details:
**Seagram Building**
Mies's 38-story bronze-and-glass skyscraper at 375 Park Avenue in Manhattan (1958), designed with Philip Johnson, who did interiors including the Four Seasons Restaurant. Non-structural bronze I-beams on the exterior express the hidden steel frame, the tower sits back behind an open plaza, and the window blinds were limited to three positions (open, half, closed) to keep the facade uniform.

**Farnsworth House**
Mies's glass-walled weekend retreat (1951) in Plano, Illinois, outside Chicago, built for the physician Edith Farnsworth. It is a white-painted steel frame raised about five feet on stilts above a floodplain, with floor-to-ceiling glass walls hung with curtains. The only enclosed area is a central "core" holding the kitchen, bathrooms, and fireplace.

**"Less is more"**
The minimalist maxim most associated with Mies, summing up his reduced, unornamented style. He is also linked to the saying "God is in the details."

**Last director of the Bauhaus**
Mies led the influential German design school from 1930 until he closed it in 1933 under Nazi pressure. He later emigrated to the United States, where he became a leading figure of the International Style.

**Barcelona Pavilion and Barcelona chair**
The German Pavilion that Mies designed for the 1929 International Exposition in Barcelona: a flowing open plan of freestanding walls of marble, onyx, and glass under a flat roof on slender chrome columns. A Georg Kolbe statue titled Alba (Dawn) stands in a small reflecting pool. For it, Mies and Lilly Reich designed the Barcelona chair, a leather-cushioned seat on an X-shaped steel frame, and a matching table.

**Villa Tugendhat**
The house Mies designed (1930) in Brno, Czechoslovakia, for Fritz and Grete Tugendhat. Its main living space has a translucent onyx wall, and its huge windows facing the garden could be lowered into the floor. Mies and Lilly Reich designed the cantilevered Brno chair and the Tugendhat chair for it.

**Lake Shore Drive Apartments**
Mies's pair of steel-and-glass apartment towers at 860–880 Lake Shore Drive in Chicago (1951), overlooking Lake Michigan and exemplifying his "skin and bones" architecture. Their exterior I-beam mullions are non-structural, which made them controversial as decoration on a supposedly honest steel frame.

**S. R. Crown Hall**
The home of the architecture school at the Illinois Institute of Technology (1956), where Mies headed the architecture department and taught. It is a single huge open room with glass walls, its roof hung from exposed steel girders above, and it was built on the site of the demolished Mecca Flats apartment building.

**Lilly Reich**
The German designer who was Mies's longtime collaborator in the 1920s and 1930s. She co-designed furniture and interiors for the Barcelona Pavilion and the Villa Tugendhat, including the Barcelona and Brno chairs.

**Chicago Federal Center**
Mies's complex of dark steel-and-glass federal buildings in downtown Chicago. Its plaza features Alexander Calder's bright red sculpture Flamingo, whose color contrasts with the black buildings.

**Neue Nationalgalerie**
The New National Gallery in Berlin's Kulturforum (1968), Mies's last major work, nicknamed a "temple of light and glass." A glass hall sits beneath a vast steel roof supported by only eight columns, and the artist Jenny Holzer later installed an LED text work on its ceiling.

**Lafayette Park**
A residential development in Detroit with townhouses and high-rise apartments, containing the largest collection of Mies-designed buildings anywhere.

**Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial Library**
The central public library of Washington, D.C., Mies's only library. It was completed in 1972, a few years after his death in 1969, and was recently renovated to bring in more natural light.

**Weissenhof Estate and the Deutscher Werkbund**
Mies, as a leader of the Deutscher Werkbund, directed the 1927 Weissenhof Estate exhibition in Stuttgart. It was a model housing development featuring buildings by leading modernists, including Le Corbusier and Walter Gropius.
